You reach for your phone during a quiet moment.
Silence means I am missing something.
I can notice this urge before deciding.
Put the phone down for 30 seconds and notice the urge.
Move one distracting app off your home screen.
When I reach for my phone without a purpose, I will name the urge before deciding.
A message arrives and your chest tightens.
This feeling means something terrible will happen.
A feeling is information; it is not a prediction.
Look around and name three things you can see; feel your feet on the floor.
Give yourself a quiet place to read difficult messages.
When a message unsettles me, I will orient to the room before replying.
Someone does not reply to your message.
They do not care about me.
I am noticing a story about rejection. I do not know yet.
Say: I am noticing the thought that… Then return to what you were doing.
Choose a message-checking window rather than repeatedly refreshing.
When I interpret silence as rejection, I will name the interpretation and wait.
You consider a career your family did not expect.
If I disappoint them, I am a bad person.
I can care about them and examine this rule.
Identify one inherited rule. Ask when it helps, and when it limits you.
Find one trusted person who can discuss your options without deciding for you.
When I hear an inherited should, I will examine its costs and benefits.
You scroll after a tiring workday.
I need this; it is the only way to switch off.
I may be seeking rest, novelty or connection.
Notice what you get immediately from the habit and what it costs later.
Make an alternative source of rest easy to reach.
When I want to scroll after work, I will first try two minutes of another kind of rest.
A notification interrupts a meaningful task.
I can decide what deserves an interruption.
Try one ten-minute focus block with nonessential notifications off.
Keep essential contacts available; silence one nonessential channel.
When I begin a focused task, I will silence one avoidable interruption.
An old response returns after a good day.
A slip tells me about a cue or a difficult condition.
Review one experiment: what happened, what helped, what got in the way?
Make the next action smaller or easier.
When a practice does not work, I will adjust one condition and try again.
A friend posts a major success.
Their progress proves I am behind.
Their public moment does not measure my whole life.
Notice the comparison; choose one personally meaningful next action.
Mute one source of repeated unhelpful comparison for a week.
When comparison pulls me into checking, I will return to one task I value.
You agree to something you do not have capacity for.
If I say no, they will reject me.
I can be considerate and be clear about my capacity.
Practise: I cannot do that today; I can offer this instead.
Delay nonurgent commitments until you have checked your time.
When asked for a nonurgent favour, I will check my capacity before agreeing.
An uncomfortable feeling appears during a task.
I must get rid of this feeling before I act.
I can allow some discomfort and take a small step.
Name the feeling without judging it. Take a safe, manageable next step.
Reduce the task to a version you can approach today.
When discomfort makes me avoid a manageable task, I will do its smallest safe step.
You make a mistake at work.
One mistake deserves a specific explanation.
Separate the event, your interpretation, evidence and another explanation.
Ask for specific feedback instead of guessing what others think.
When I say always or never about myself, I will describe the specific event.
Two choices compete for your time.
I should do whatever makes me look successful.
I can choose a direction that matters to me.
Status cue → borrowed goal → restless pursuit
Choose a value such as care, curiosity or integrity. Name one visible action that expresses it.
Put a small values-based action into your existing routine.
When I choose a task today, I will connect it to a value I personally endorse.
You feel an urge to send an angry reply.
I must make them understand immediately.
I can pause and choose a response that serves the conversation.
Draft without sending. Re-read later and identify your actual request.
Use a draft or delayed-send option where available.
When I feel ready to send an angry reply, I will save a draft and revisit it.
You notice a pattern but still act on it.
Noticing and acting differently are separate skills.
Compare your first and latest attempts. Choose one pattern to keep practising.
Remove one remaining barrier to your chosen response.
When I notice a loop, I will practise one alternative rather than demand instant change.
You want to practise but forget when life gets busy.
I can attach a tiny practice to an existing cue.
Busy day → forgotten intention → no practice
After an existing routine, practise one minute of noticing or a chosen action.
Place a simple cue where the routine happens.
After I finish my morning drink, I will name one action that matters today.
You react sharply after a short night.
I am simply an angry person.
My current capacity and circumstances may matter.
Notice energy and available support before judging your character.
Protect a realistic wind-down window or ask for help with one demand.
When I am depleted, I will reduce one avoidable demand before a hard conversation.
Your usual trigger appears outside the app.
I only know this when I am calm.
I can practise one small response in this context.
Real cue → old response → familiar outcome
Choose a low-stakes real moment. Try your planned response and observe the result.
Keep your plan visible at the place the trigger usually appears.
When my chosen trigger appears, I will try my smallest alternative and observe.
Your workplace repeatedly interrupts your breaks.
I must fix my mindset and cope with everything.
Some demands need a practical or collective change.
Map what you control, what you can influence and what requires support.
Make one realistic request for support, resources or a boundary.
When a problem exceeds personal practice, I will identify an appropriate source of support.
A familiar habit returns during stress.
I can resume from the next opportunity.
Describe the slip neutrally. Identify one cue and restart with a smaller action.
Prepare a fallback version for difficult days.
When I miss a practice, I will use the one-minute version at the next opportunity.
Someone presents evidence against an opinion you hold.
Changing my mind means losing myself.
I can examine evidence without abandoning my dignity.
State what evidence would change your view. Read one credible alternative fairly.
Keep a source-checking habit before sharing strong claims.
When a claim fits my beliefs, I will still check its source and uncertainty.
I should now be permanently free of conditioning.
I have practices to keep learning and choosing.
Compare observations, keep one helpful practice and make a plan for difficult days.
Choose a weekly review cue and one person or resource for support.
When an old pattern returns, I will notice, choose a small action and adjust the conditions.
